about.lead1: Hey, I’m Artem, a product designer with 5+ years of experience in fintech, B2B, B2C and SaaS products. Based in Prague.
about.lead2: Since 2021 I’ve worked on 85+ projects at Bozhenko Design Club and with international clients on Upwork, taking products from research and hypotheses to tested, ready-to-build interfaces.
about.lead3: With a degree in software engineering, I design with implementation in mind and work closely with developers, from design systems to handoff.
about.toolkit.label: Current toolkit
art.a-catalog-is-needed-where: A catalog is needed where people don’t know exactly what they’re looking for: they narrow the selection step by step until they reach the right item. If they know the name, search is enough.
art.a-large-set-of-items: A large set of items that users browse, search, filter and sort.
art.a-list-of-the-patterns: A list of the patterns the task is made of, a product × criterion table, annotated references (what you take, what you rejected and why) and a list of questions nobody asked when the task was first discussed.
art.a-place-to-collect-items: A place to collect items, review and change them, then confirm them all at once.
art.a-reference-is-a-single: A reference is a single example of someone else’s solution: a screen, a flow or a piece of copy. Benchmarking is the process of comparing how different products solve the same task and working out why a solution works.
art.a-reference-without-a-note: A reference without a note is just a picture. For each one, write down what fits your task, what doesn’t and why.
art.a-user-s-personal-space: A user’s personal space for profile, security, billing and preferences.
art.adjacent-products-the-same-category: Adjacent products. The same category, another price segment or audience.
art.ask-three-questions-which-user: Ask three questions: which user and business task does it solve, what happens before and after it, and is it made for an audience like yours?
art.behind-this-is-jakob-s: Behind this is Jakob’s Law: people spend most of their time in other products and expect yours to work the same way. Structure, behavior and controls should feel familiar; your own visual style doesn’t get in the way of that.
art.below-i-ve-drawn-a: Below I’ve drawn a simplified funnel for each service type.
art.benchmarks-don-t-prove-a: Benchmarks don’t prove a solution will work for you. The final check is user testing and analytics after launch.
art.choosing-a-payment-method-confirming: Choosing a payment method, confirming the amount and seeing a clear result.
art.combine-sources-walk-through-the: Combine sources. Walk through the flows yourself to see errors, emails and what happens on return. Use screen libraries like Mobbin to compare one pattern across dozens of products. Check usability research from Baymard Institute and Nielsen Norman Group.
art.compare-flows-by-the-same: Compare flows by the same criteria in a product × criterion table. What everyone shares is the market norm. Where solutions differ is room for your own hypotheses.
art.compare-scenarios-not-whole-products: Compare scenarios, not whole products. First describe yours without any interface: what the user wants to get and which steps it takes.
art.constraints-remove-what-doesn-t: Constraints. Remove what doesn’t fit the technical, legal and resource limits, however well it works for others.
art.constraints-technical-legal-and-reso: Constraints. Technical, legal and resource limits, plus the client’s expectations. They keep you from searching for the impossible, and later they filter what you’ve collected.
art.context-product-type-b2b-or: Context. Product type, B2B or B2C, audience experience, devices.
art.describe-the-scenario-and-decide: Describe the scenario and decide whose products to look at
art.everyone-collects-references-but-too: Everyone collects references, but too often it ends with a folder of nice-looking screens that does nothing to solve the task. In this guide I’ll show a different way to search: one where every find answers a specific question.
art.example-we-re-designing-a: Example. We’re designing a trip planning app. A tourist doesn’t know what the city offers, so the list of places is a catalog. A place page with photos and opening hours is a detail page. The places added to the trip work like a cart. Now references can come from online stores and booking services, not only from other travel apps.
art.exception-in-niches-with-complex: Exception. In niches with complex business logic (geo services, social networks, messengers) abstraction helps less. There you look for proven solutions from direct analogs: the systems are too complex to invent the connections from scratch.
art.it-speeds-up-collecting-not: It speeds up collecting, not thinking. Notes, comparison and cuts are still my job.
art.label-each-screen-right-away: Label each screen right away: product, step, pattern.
art.market-leaders-from-any-industry: Market leaders. From any industry. Their solutions are usually backed by research.
art.mobbin-has-an-mcp-server: Mobbin has an MCP server, so Claude can search its library of real screens and flows for me. I describe the task, send a screenshot or attach a brief, and get examples from other products with links back to Mobbin.
art.most-tasks-are-assembled-from: Most tasks are assembled from parts that have been solved many times: a catalog, a detail page, a cart. People know how these parts work from other products and expect yours to work the same way (Jakob’s Law). So name the patterns in your task and look for references to each one. Below is a map of the common ones.
art.nav.label: Article
art.neighboring-fields-the-same-mechanic: Neighboring fields. The same mechanic elsewhere: document checks exist in banks, car sharing and home rentals.
art.once-you-know-the-stage: Once you know the stage, you stop looking for “fintech references” and start looking for “onboarding and activation in SaaS”. The pool of suitable products grows beyond your industry, and the search itself gets more precise: you’re comparing solutions to the same task.
art.one-person-s-selection-stays: One person’s selection stays a hypothesis until others have seen it. Show the analysis to the product manager, the developers and the client: they know priorities and constraints you may not.
art.product-types-with-conventions-that: Product types with conventions that users already know.
art.run-what-you-ve-collected: Run what you’ve collected through two filters.
art.save-everything-you-like-and: Save everything you like and don’t judge it yet. Filter too early and you miss an unexpected find from another niche.
art.shot.alt: The Mobbin connector page in Claude: connected, with the tools search_flows, search_screens and search_sections
art.sign-up-sign-in-and: Sign-up, sign in and the checks that confirm a user’s identity.
art.skill.status-selected: Text selected, copy it with the keyboard
art.slider.label: Funnels by service type
art.start-with-products-of-the: Start with products of the same type. Then check which patterns from this list they contain: most custom flows still include a catalog, a detail page or a form.
art.step-by-step-input-where: Step-by-step input where each answer shapes the next step and the final result.
art.stores-and-any-services-with: Stores and any services with a catalog and a process of choosing and buying
art.the-core-flows-of-a: The core flows of a product, built around its own rules and data.
art.the-first-run-experience-that: The first-run experience that leads a new user to the product’s core value.
art.the-page-with-full-information: The page with full information about one item, where users decide what to do next.
art.the-service-type-and-the: The service type and the funnel stage define the goal of a screen, and so they define which products are comparable. SaaS onboarding and a store checkout solve different tasks, even if both look like a multi-step form.
art.then-look-for-products-that: Then look for products that already solve it, moving from near to far:
art.three-things-worth-knowing-before: Three things worth knowing before you start
art.to-keep-every-search-in: To keep every search in the order of this guide, I packed the steps into a Claude skill. It turns a task into search queries, checks each result against one criterion and says what it did not find.
art.to-use-it-download-the: To use it, download the ZIP, upload it in Claude under Customize → Skills and connect Mobbin.
art.users-learned-these-products-from: Users learned these products from the market leaders and expect yours to work the same way. Start with direct competitors.
art.value-and-cost-weigh-how: Value and cost. Weigh how much a solution helps the user against what it costs to build. A large feature with no clear value is the first to go.
art.what-matters-is-how-a: What matters is how a solution works, not only how it looks. Copy the visuals and you get a pretty screen. Understand the logic and you get an idea you can adapt to your own product.
